quote: Beweise, dass [-?-] in der Reihe $f(0)\ f(1)\ f(2)\ ..$ wenigstens eine Primzahl vorkommt.
english: Prove that at least one prime number occurs in the sequence f(0), f(1), f(2), ...
topic: Notes on solving linear Diophantine equations in primes (including twin primes), a plan to treat this via Weierstrass's theory of elementary factors and the Riemann–Roch theorem, primes among the values of a polynomial, remarks on the nature of mathematics, and a sketch of a proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra.

triage.modern_statement: Let f ∈ Z[x] be a nonconstant polynomial with positive leading coefficient. Assume f is irreducible over Z and that the values f(0), f(1), f(2), … have no common factor greater than 1 (no fixed prime divisor). Prove that at least one f(n) with n ≥ 0 is prime. Applying the statement to the shifted polynomials f(x+N) shows this is equivalent to f taking infinitely many prime values. That is the Bunyakovsky (Bouniakowsky) conjecture of 1857. For linear f it is Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions. Hilbert's exact hypotheses are illegible ([-?-]), so this assumes he meant the standard ones.
triage.answered_by: Not answered in general. Only degree 1 is settled, by Dirichlet's theorem (1837). For degree 2 and higher the question is still open. Even the simplest case, infinitely many primes of the form n^2+1, is open; it is one of the four problems Landau called unattackable in 1912. This is not one of Hilbert's 23 published problems as such, although his 8th problem (the Riemann hypothesis, Goldbach and twin primes) is closely related.

evidence.claim: Bunyakovsky's conjecture says that if f satisfies conditions (1)–(3) (positive leading coefficient, irreducible, no common factor of the values), then f(n) is prime for infinitely many n. An equivalent, weaker-looking form says f(n) is prime for at least one n, which is exactly Hilbert's formulation.
Bunyakovsky stated the conjecture in 1857. It gives conditions under which an integer polynomial in one variable should have infinitely many prime values.
These conjectures (Bunyakovsky, Schinzel–Sierpinski) have been open for many years.

Landau listed four problems at the 1912 ICM, including whether there are infinitely many primes of the form n^2+1. Pintz's 2009 survey says all of them are still open and reviews recent partial results.
Pintz's survey says Landau's problems are all still open and focuses on recent partial results.

triage.why: The page context (primes represented by polynomials, alongside linear Diophantine equations in primes and twin primes) and the wording 'at least one prime in f(0), f(1), …' match the 'at least one value is prime' form of Bunyakovsky's conjecture. That form is equivalent to the 'infinitely many primes' form. The case of linear f is Dirichlet's theorem. For degree 2 and higher, including n^2+1, the problem is open and is still studied: Pintz's 2009 survey covers partial results on Landau's problems. Confidence is medium rather than high because the illegible [-?-] hides Hilbert's exact hypotheses on f. He might also have meant only a special case, such as linear f, which Dirichlet's theorem settles.
